title: Gothic Revival
description: The Gothic Revival entered Bucharest's architectural scene mainly in the second half of the 19th century. At the time, the capital was going through a process of modernisation and Westernisation. The style arrived, however, more as a selective, filtered reinterpretation, adapted to local requirements.

Under the influence of currents from Western Europe — the Gothic revival championed by Augustus Pugin in England and Viollet-le-Duc in France — Romanian architects began to adopt elements of this rediscovered vocabulary. The message went beyond aesthetics: the aim was a Bucharest with historical legitimacy and European aspirations, a deliberate act of cultural borrowing for the capital of the United Principalities.

Defining architectural features:
  • Pointed arches, formed by a broken arch, are the defining element of the Gothic style. They appear mostly on façades, allowing slender windows with wide openings, but also inside, in the form of portals;
  • Tall towers with spires are another element taken from the Gothic repertoire, once again emphasising the building's height;
  • Stained-glass windows, especially rose windows and floral motifs;
  • Buttresses and pinnacles – present in Bucharest's urban fabric more as decoration than as structure.

Bucharest does not have many buildings displaying the elements above, as the Gothic Revival appears mostly in religious architecture and public buildings, but a few residential examples are worth mentioning.
Representative buildings:

buildings.name: "H.I. Rieber" Carriage Factory, Strada Romulus nr. 15-17, Bucharest

title: Neoclassical
description: In Bucharest, Neoclassicism is one of the most visible architectural styles, shaping the face of the city throughout the 19th century. The capital was undergoing a profound transformation, in which architecture was meant to come as close as possible to Western European standards. This style answered exactly that need for belonging, and was a perfect tool for expressing those aspirations.

Through a language of reason, order and the legacy of Greco-Roman antiquity, filtered through the 18th-century Enlightenment, Neoclassicism reinterpreted the image of the city as an expression of legitimacy. Compared with the Gothic Revival, associated with spirituality and the medieval heritage, Neoclassicism conveyed a democratic, secular message, typical of a modern state with institutions, banks and aristocratic palaces, while also offering historical legitimacy, order and stability.

In Romania, the style arrived with the return of architects trained in Paris or Vienna. Alexandru Orăscu and Michel Sanjouand brought this vocabulary to Bucharest, passing it through a local filter, with different materials and craft traditions. A preference for eclecticism made pure Neoclassicism relatively rare. Even so, a Neoclassical vocabulary emerged that makes the style easy to recognise.

Defining architectural features:
  • The colonnade (a row of columns with Doric and/or Corinthian capitals);
  • The classical pediment (triangular, with or without decoration);
  • Strict symmetry around a central axis (windows, pilasters and ornaments follow this invisible line).

All these elements seek to evoke the gravity and rigour of the ancient temple, while embracing the Enlightenment belief that beauty is rooted in mathematical order and reason. A typical façade in this style in Bucharest is composed of pilasters (flattened columns built into the wall), with an entablature made up of an architrave, friezes and moulded cornices finishing each storey of the building. Most of the time, the ground-floor walls are treated differently, with masonry blocks and deep joints that give weight and mass to the base of the building, leaving the upper floors to look lighter, with larger windows and more decoration.

Walking through the city, the Neoclassical style is easy to spot in public and educational buildings, as well as in residences built for the elite. Notable examples include the University of Bucharest, designed by Alexandru Orăscu, with a façade defined by a portico with Ionic columns, a central pediment and strict symmetry. Among residential buildings, the Știrbei Palace and the Ghica-Tei Palace show how Bucharest's elite adopted the Neoclassical style to assert their belonging to the European world.

Representative buildings:
  • University of Bucharest | 1869 | arch. Alexandru Orăscu | Bd. Regina Elisabeta 4-12
    portico with Ionic columns, central pediment with allegorical bas-relief
  • Ghica-Tei Palace | 1822 | arch. Xavier Villacrosse | Strada Doamna Ghica 5
    suburban villa with a loggia of semicircular arches and Ionic pilasters, a symbol of residential Neoclassicism with Viennese-Italian influences

title: Art Nouveau/ Secession
description: Art Nouveau entered Bucharest's local repertoire between the end of the 19th century and the first decade of the 20th century, a period later known as “La Belle Époque”. Cultural effervescence and rapid industrialisation made it necessary for cities to expand. In this moment of profound change, architecture also sought to move beyond historicist and Neoclassical patterns, looking for a way to express the energy of the period.

Across Europe, the style went by several names: “Jugendstil” in Germany and the Netherlands, “Secession” in Austria and Hungary, “stile Liberty” in Italy. The movement aimed to follow nature literally, adopting the curved line and organic ornament as the defining elements of artistic creation. The style reached Bucharest with Romanian architects returning home from their studies in Paris or Vienna, and through builders brought in from the West to carry out commissions for the local bourgeoisie.

The Art Nouveau façade has an undulating look and an asymmetrical composition. Its free, energetic “whiplash” curve makes the style easy to identify. Windows do not follow a strict arrangement either; instead, there is a play of volumes stepping back and forward in the plane of the façade. Everything is arranged organically, in relief, from the volume itself down to the decoration, which takes the form of floral and plant-like profiles. Materials are varied too: stucco, cast iron and glazed ceramics cover friezes, cornices, brackets and window surrounds.

Defining architectural features:
  • Window and door surrounds often bear sculpted female faces called mascarons. These female figures carry a symbolism closely tied to Art Nouveau iconography: their flowing hair is meant to convey the unconstrained force of nature and fertility as a creative principle.
  • Plant-like ironwork follows the same logic in metal. Balustrades, window grilles and canopies over entrances are cast in iron to reproduce the look of stems with leaves and buds. Although metal was at the time associated with an industrial aesthetic, Art Nouveau used it to create an aesthetic paradox.
  • Colour comes from stained glass and glazed ceramics. Colour, too, becomes an aesthetic paradox, moving from religious architecture to the private home. Light enters the interior in coloured floral shapes (the typical colours being yellow, green and teal) and is reflected in the glaze of the ceramic decoration on the façade.
  • The vertical, often pointed, massing of buildings in this style can also be recognised by turrets (octagonal towers covered in slate or zinc scales), ceramic pinnacles and curved bay windows.

References for this style include the “House with Lions” on Strada Vasile Lascăr and the Macca-Vilacrosse Passage. A representative area for this style is the one bounded by Strada Polonă, Strada Dumbrava Roșie and Bulevardul Dacia.

Representative buildings:
  • Cantacuzino Palace | 1901–1903 | arch. Ioan D. Berindei | Calea Victoriei 141
  • Athénée Palace Hotel | 1912–1914 | arch. Théophile Bradeau | Strada Episcopiei 1-3
  • Romulus Porescu House | 1905 | arch. Dimitrie Maimarolu | Strada Doctor Paleologu 12
  • The house on Strada Dimitrie Racoviță | Strada Dimitrie Racoviță
  • Amzei Church | Piața Amzei

title: Eclectic
description: In the mid-19th century, Bucharest was changing rapidly, driven by a project to Westernise the capital. The architects of the period, most of whom had studied in the West (France, Italy, Germany), sought to meet this need through a current that refused to use a single architectural vocabulary. Eclecticism is not, however, a style without vision; rather, it was conceived out of a wish to give cultural legitimacy to a newly formed state. Borrowing elements from the repertoire of other parts of Western Europe, the style reached its peak between 1860 and 1900 (with isolated examples up to 1915).

Defining architectural features:
  • As a fundamental principle, juxtaposition is the main tool for combining elements from different historical styles in the same composition.
  • The classical orders of antiquity (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian) are used mainly to articulate façades vertically, giving them hierarchy and rhythm. The pediment, also inherited from the Greek temple, returns obsessively above portals and windows.
  • The moulded cornice, supported by carved brackets, marks the top edge and balances the composition (an element borrowed from the vocabulary of Roman palazzetti).
  • The contrast between smooth and rough wall surfaces suggests a stable building: a rusticated ground floor (the plinth) and delicately decorated upper floors. Rustication further articulates the façade, while garlands and medallions communicate the owner's status and aspirations directly to the viewer, turning the house into their calling card.

A typical eclectic Bucharest building might have a rusticated plinth inspired by Renaissance architecture, pilasters with Corinthian capitals (in the classical style), windows with pediments of alternating geometry (triangular and semicircular) in the Baroque tradition, and a bracketed cornice. Such juxtaposition still follows the principle mentioned above: a composition with a clear vertical logic, from massive to delicate.

Within Bucharest's built fabric, the examples form a coherent route through the city centre, from the CEC Palace (designed by Paul Gottereau and opened in 1900) to the Romanian Athenaeum (designed by Albert Galleron and completed in 1888) and the Cantacuzino Palace (designed by Ion D. Berindei in 1903). All these buildings used this style to become a mirror of Western Europe in a Bucharest marked by the chaos typical of the years when Romania was becoming a kingdom.

Representative buildings:
  • CEC Palace | 1900 | arch. Paul Gottereau | Calea Victoriei 11
  • Romanian Athenaeum | 1888 | arch. Albert Galleron | Strada Benjamin Franklin 1
  • Cantacuzino Palace | 1903 | arch. Ion D. Berindei | Calea Victoriei 141
  • University Palace | 1857–1869 | arch. Alexandru Orăscu | Bulevardul Mihail Kogălniceanu 36-46
  • Palace of Justice | 1895 | arch. Albert Ballu & Louis Pierre Alexis Bernier | Bulevardul Independenței 5
  • Post Office Palace | 1900 | arch. Alexandru Săvulescu | Calea Victoriei 12
  • National Bank Palace | 1885–1900 | arch. Cassien Bernard & Albert Galleron | Strada Lipscani 25

title: Mediterranean Picturesque
description: Emerging in the interwar period, the Mediterranean picturesque style shaped the built fabric out of a need for a more relaxed, warmer and brighter style. Inspired by the building traditions of the Mediterranean basin, it can be said not to belong to any particular school, but to find its vocabulary by directly adopting the forms and materials of southern Europe. Places such as Italy, Spain or the Dalmatian coast became not just tourist attractions, but a way of life people wanted to bring into the city. The style reached its peak between 1920 and 1940.

Defining architectural features:
  • The picturesque massing is deliberately irregular, with freely articulated volumes, towers attached to low buildings and terraces projecting from the façade. Like an organic silhouette, this type of building blends perfectly into the rocky landscape typical of the region.
  • Open galleries with round arches, on the upper floor or the ground floor, usually create in-between spaces between inside and outside. This element is borrowed mainly from the Roman architectural vocabulary.
  • Warm materials are another element that makes the style recognisable. Terracotta roofs, façades rendered in natural colours (ochre, sienna, lime white), and window frames and shutters painted in plant-like shades come together in an ensemble that evokes the picturesque charm of Tuscany or Provence. Other typical materials are blue and yellow glazed ceramics and ceramic decorative elements (planters, fountains).

In Bucharest, the buildings relevant to this style are found in the city's residential neighbourhoods of detached houses. Streets such as Șoseaua Kiseleff, Aleea Alexandru or Bulevardul Aviatorilor are dotted with houses with arched loggias, terracotta roofs and gardens with stone fountains. The Dorobanți neighbourhood (especially Strada Paris and Strada Madrid) still has a remarkable density of villas with a distinctly Mediterranean character.

Representative buildings:
  • Museum of Maps | Strada Londra 39

title: Industrial Architecture
description: In Bucharest, industrial architecture can be read by following the city's concentric rings; it is considered the main pillar of the city's modernisation from a market town along a river into today's European capital. Arranged in concentric rings, the factories, halls, warehouses and plants are fragments of history and works of architecture that speak not only of the building capabilities of their periods, but also of a language of their own, directly associated with those periods. The features of this architecture therefore cannot be captured by a single vocabulary.

The first ring/period covers the years between 1850 and 1900. With a vocabulary inspired by Victorian factories and the Austro-Hungarian Gründerzeit, factories were built with exposed metal structures, walls of exposed polychrome brick and pitched roofs with glazed sections (usually facing north). Following the city's old “barriers” (toll gates), the most representative structures of this kind are the CFR Grivița Workshops, the Municipal Slaughterhouse and Assan's Mill.

The interwar period brought another wave of innovation, including reinforced concrete used on an industrial scale. This new use of concrete created a new visual vocabulary, with geometric modernist façades, ribbon windows and towers marking the factory entrances. Skylights were arranged to flood the new halls with diffuse light. Continuing the first ring, buildings such as the Malaxa Factory and the Leonida Works remain the best-preserved buildings in the modernist style.

The socialist era, between 1948 and 1989, brought a change of scale. Colossal volumes were grouped into plant or industrial platform complexes. The new vocabulary had to convey the monumental aspirations of the time, as an expression of collective grandeur. To build such massive, repetitive structures as quickly as possible, prefabricated reinforced concrete elements were used, along with steel on a large scale. Among the most telling examples are the IMGB, Republica and Electroaparataj platforms. These were located on another ring of urban development, which was later extended in turn.

Today, industrial structures are built on the city's periurban fringe, while the existing heritage is being reconsidered and increasingly given new uses, adapted to the economic profile of the contemporary city and the needs of a growing population.

Representative buildings:
  • CFR Grivița Workshops | 1872–1890 | Calea Griviței 193
  • Rahova / Steaua Brewery | 1895–1910 | Calea Rahovei 147
  • Timpuri Noi Factory / former Malaxa Factory | 1921–1938 | Calea Văcărești 391
  • Leonida Works | 1920–1935 | Calea Rahovei 266
  • IMGB — Bucharest Heavy Machinery Enterprise | 1950–1960 | Bulevardul Metalurgiei
  • Republica Factory | 1948–1965 | Șoseaua Colentina 6
  • Combinatul Fondului Plastic | 1964 / converted 2010+ | Calea Floreasca 160

title: Romanian Revival
description: Emerging as the modern state consolidated after its proclamation as the Kingdom of Romania (1881), the Romanian Revival (Neo-Romanian) style was born out of a deliberate effort by late 19th-century architects to build a unified and coherent national identity. It was theorised and put into practice by architects such as Ion Mincu, Petre Antonescu, Nicolae Ghika-Budești and Cristofi Cerchez. The first of them, after finishing his studies in Paris, returned home and used medieval architecture and folk art as sources of inspiration for this new architectural vocabulary.

Defining architectural features:
  • Trefoil arches framing windows, porches and loggias are one of the most recognisable elements of the Romanian Revival style. This element was taken from the language of the great monastic ensembles of the 15th and 16th centuries (Curtea de Argeș Monastery, Voroneț).
  • Alongside these arches comes an equally important element: the foișor, a raised open porch or loggia. As a transitional space, it is inherited from boyar architecture and has no equivalent in Western architectural language.
  • Twisted columns with capitals decorated with plant motifs, as well as carved stone window and door surrounds bearing similar symbols, give the façades a rich, organic rhythm. Rosettes, vine tendrils and octagonal towers adorn the façades and give them a natural rhythm.
  • In terms of materials, the style stands out for its contrasting collage of textures. One example is the addition of coloured glazed ceramic elements (discs, panels) to the masonry. Arranged in bands or as details of window surrounds, they contrast strongly with the rough texture of the façade (dressed stone or exposed brick). Wood is used for brackets, balustrades and joinery, carved with geometric or plant motifs that echo the ornamental vocabulary of Romanian folk art.

In Bucharest, the Romanian Revival style reached maturity in the interwar period. It left behind buildings with important programmes — banks, town halls, administrative palaces and university buildings — becoming a tool for defining cultural legitimacy, as the state needed to assert both tradition and the historical continuity in which the Romanian people had formed.

Representative buildings:
  • National Museum of the Romanian Peasant | 1912–1941 | arch. Nicolae Ghika-Budești | Șoseaua Pavel D. Kiseleff 3
  • “Ion Mincu” University of Architecture and Urbanism — old building | 1912–1927 | arch. Grigore Cerchez | Strada Academiei 18-20
  • Ion Mincu Memorial House | c. 1890 (restoration and extension) | arch. Ion Mincu | Strada Pictor Arthur Verona 19

buildings.name: Zottu Villa, Strada C. A. Rosetti 7

title: Modernism
description: The first decades of the 20th century brought substantial changes to European architecture, driven by a desire for a radical break with the past. The modernist movement that grew out of the studios of Le Corbusier, Walter Gropius and Mies van der Rohe promoted an honest architecture without ornament, in which function, not style, would dictate how interior spaces were organised. Bucharest at that time was relatively well connected to the West through a generation of architects who had already studied abroad in the 1920s. In this context, modernism was quickly adopted by figures such as Horia Creangă, Duliu Marcu, Marcel Iancu and Octav Doicescu. The style's peak can be placed between 1925 and 1945, alongside other styles such as Art Deco and the Mediterranean picturesque.

Defining architectural elements:
  • The main element of the modernist vocabulary is the abandonment of ornament. Façades are designed as smooth white surfaces, without decorated cornices, pilasters or stucco. The result is a pure volume, a cube or a rectangular block that asserts itself through contrast. Cantilevered balconies, with linear balustrades of tubular steel or perforated concrete, give the façades rhythm and create a play of light and shadow.
  • The ribbon window, which provides a continuous horizontal opening, was made possible only by a reinforced concrete frame of columns and beams, which relieves the exterior walls of their load-bearing role. On the same principle, the corner window changes the relationship between outside and inside.
  • Last but not least, there is the flat roof with an accessible terrace. It replaces the traditional pitched roof, offering additional living space and suggesting the modern horizon. Concrete pillars lift the volume off the ground, creating a permeable ground floor and free pedestrian movement, as well as the impression that the new building is floating.

In Bucharest, the ARO Building and the Scala Building on Bulevardul Magheru, designed by Horia Creangă in the 1930s, are the most coherent syntheses of the style. On Calea Victoriei stands the Telephone Palace, which brought American-inspired modernism into Bucharest's fabric. Also worth mentioning are Marcel Iancu's villas in the Floreasca neighbourhood, which add an expressionist note, with dynamic volumes and a tense, sculptural façade. All these examples reinforce Bucharest's heterogeneous character and mirror the Romanian capital's path from market town to cosmopolitan city.

Representative buildings:
  • ARO / Patria Building | 1931–1935 | arch. Horia Creangă | Bulevardul Gheorghe Magheru 12-14
  • Malaxa / Scala Building | 1935 | arch. Horia Creangă | Bulevardul Gheorghe Magheru 2
  • Telephone Palace | 1933 | arch. Louis Weeks & Walter Froy | Calea Victoriei 37
  • Iancu House | 1933 | arch. Marcel Iancu

title: Art Deco
description: The 1925 Exhibition of Decorative Arts in Paris introduced a new style: Art Deco. Compared with Art Nouveau, which had its origins in nature, this style used mathematical precision, geometry and high-quality materials to express the new pace of life of the 1920s. It was also heavily influenced by the period's fascination with archaeological discoveries from Egyptian and pre-Columbian civilisations.

In Bucharest, it was enthusiastically adopted by interwar architects during the city's rapid expansion, as they were looking for a modern language that would not take away from the elegance of the new city. Names such as Horia Creangă, George Matei Cantacuzino and Duliu Marcu are associated with this period.

Defining architectural features:
  • The geometrisation of ornament is undoubtedly the defining element of the style. Compositions made of zigzags, triangles, parallel lines and fan motifs enriched the city's decorative vocabulary. Horizontal friezes with zigzag motifs, parapets with geometric cut-outs and stylised female figures are just a few examples of the style's recognisable vocabulary.
  • As with Art Nouveau, façades are articulated by continuous vertical bands meant to emphasise the building's height. The progressive setbacks of the upper floors (ziggurat-style) are inspired directly by the aesthetics of New York skyscrapers. Window surrounds are also stepped.
  • Materials considered noble also play an important role in this style. Coloured marble, polished stoneware, cast bronze, anodised aluminium and geometric mosaic are used to finish both exterior façades and interiors.

Buildings from this period are scattered across Bucharest's fabric, with some areas where they are easier to find. On Bulevardul Magheru there are the Scala Cinema (geometric façade and a monumental cast-bronze entrance) and the Ambasador Hotel (strong vertical rhythm, geometric cast-bronze ironwork). Representative ensembles for this style include the villas in the Floreasca and Dorobanți neighbourhoods.

In Bucharest's urban composition, Art Deco speaks of the effervescent, elegant and cosmopolitan character of the interwar period. Adopted with a relatively short delay, it left a visible mark, creating new architectural landmarks in the city.
Representative buildings:

title: Socialist Realism
description: Socialist Realism is perhaps the most ideologically charged style, as it emerged as a direct response to the aspirations of an authoritarian regime. It did not grow organically out of stylistic evolution, but came about through a series of state decrees and decisions. With the installation of the communist regime in 1947, socialist architecture had to project a grand, classicising image, loaded with ideological symbols, while mirroring the Stalinist architecture of Moscow. Most buildings in this style in Bucharest date from the 1950s.

Defining architectural features:
  • The defining traits of this period are monumentality, control and excess. Massive volumes of exaggerated height, out of human scale, appeared on Bucharest's skyline. They were usually built around strict axial symmetry (with a tower on the axis of symmetry), with side wings arranged in an orderly, hierarchical way.
  • The architectural language of this style includes elements such as the tower, the stepped pyramid, the sphere and the bar. The purpose of these perfect, clean geometric volumes was to make the individual an insignificant point compared with the all-powerful state. The colossal scale of the new buildings aimed at nothing other than subjecting citizens, as peacefully as possible, to the new order.
  • These volumes were in turn given classicising ornaments (Corinthian pilasters and classical cornices) combined with communist iconography (the hammer and sickle, ears of wheat, cogwheels, the soldier, figures of the worker and the peasant in academic sculptural relief).
  • Equally important were narrative façades and interiors used as propaganda tools — bas-reliefs, mosaics or simple murals — all part of the vocabulary of the time.

In Bucharest, Socialist Realist urbanism only added to an already seemingly chaotic picture: the fabric of narrow streets was cut through by new wide boulevards lined with buildings that did not connect to the existing scale. Nevertheless, the period also produced works of real architectural quality, including Casa Scânteii (today the House of the Free Press), the Palace Hall, the classicising blocks on Bulevardul Magheru (the Eva Building, the ITB Building) and the residential ensembles in the Floreasca and Vatra Luminoasă neighbourhoods.

Representative buildings:
  • House of the Free Press (formerly Casa Scânteii) | 1952–1957 | arch. Horia Maicu & team | Piața Presei Libere 1

title: Socialist Modernism
description: With Stalin's exit from the political scene in 1953, a process began of criticising the architectural excess that had marked the Socialist-Stalinist period. In Romania, following Party decisions taken between 1956 and 1958, Socialist Realist decorated architecture was abandoned in favour of a state modernist-functionalist style, based largely on prefabricated elements and mass production.

Socialist Modernism as a style was also a response to the constraints of the period: accelerated, forced industrialisation led not only to massive migration from villages to cities, but also to a housing crisis that had to be solved as quickly as possible. For Bucharest, the plan was for the population to grow from 1 million to more than two million by the mid-1980s. To make this possible, Socialist Modernism had to be an “architectural style of apartment blocks”. For this reason, between 1950 and 1989 Socialist Modernism dominated architectural production in Bucharest, and it is still the most visible layer in terms of quantity today.

Defining architectural features:
  • Prefabricated concrete panels shaped the commuter neighbourhoods. These standardised slabs, cast in factories and assembled directly on site, produced façades with a monotonous rhythm, small standardised windows and continuous bands and joints.
  • The volume of buildings also became a standardised module, from the slab block (a long, narrow and tall building, often placed freely in the landscape without necessarily following the street line) to tower blocks or even curtains of blocks lining the main boulevards. This style is most visible in the Drumul Taberei, Titan, Berceni, Militari and Colentina neighbourhoods. These ensembles of thousands of homes, with green spaces and social amenities, were built in successive stages, incorporating social and cultural functions into the residential fabric.

At the same time, an authored architecture took shape: hotels, multipurpose halls, university complexes. These would later remain as very high-quality works of architecture, socialist-brutalist buildings comparable with projects in the West. This group includes the Intercontinental Hotel, the Polyvalent Hall and the Unirea Complex in Piața Unirii.

The last ten years of this period are remembered as “the decade of demolitions”, a tabula rasa that razed entire neighbourhoods (the Uranus district) and many historic monuments to make way for other buildings matching the period's aspirations (the Civic Centre, the House of the People).

Representative buildings:
  • Eva Building | c. 1960–1961 | arch. M. Dima | Bulevardul Gheorghe Magheru 7
  • Intercontinental Hotel (today Grand Hotel Bucharest) | 1968–1971 | arch. Dinu Hariton, Gheorghe Nădrag, Ion Moscu, Romeo Belea | Bulevardul Nicolae Bălcescu 4
  • “I.L. Caragiale” National Theatre | 1964–1973 | arch. Horia Maicu, Romeo Belea & team | Bulevardul Nicolae Bălcescu 2
  • Unirea Complex | 1975 | arch. Gheorghe Leahu | Piața Unirii 1

title: Brutalism
description: Of all the styles present in Bucharest, Brutalism is perhaps the most harshly judged. With exposed concrete as its signature material, it is often associated with the public discourse of the communist period. Internationally, Brutalism took shape as a coherent aesthetic movement, with well-known representatives in the United Kingdom, France, Russia and Japan. Starting from Le Corbusier's béton brut, Brutalist architecture set out to leave visible the honesty of materials and the expressiveness of the structure. The fundamental aesthetic principles of the movement were summed up by Reyner Banham in the 1950s.

Locally, the movement developed between 1960 and 1985. The cultural exchange of the period briefly coincided with movements in the West, so some Romanian architects with access to foreign magazines and books began producing Brutalist work. The defining elements they adopted constantly refer to honesty of material and the play between light and shadow.

Defining architectural features:
  • Concrete left exposed with the texture of the formwork it was cast in keeps the imprint of the boards and the grain of the wood. The result is a richly tactile surface and an honest image of how the material was put in place.
  • Another key element of the style was the exploration and exploitation of the technical capabilities of building materials, especially concrete. Casting it into cantilevered volumes, with upper floors larger than the ground floor, creates geometries that seem to defy gravity and allow the structure to become a spectacle.
  • The contrast between light and shadow is sought both through façades with narrow, deep-set windows and through large interior atriums. The skylight comes to define space around a vertical void of light, with the structure once again playing the lead role.
  • Outside, stairs and ramps take on sculptural forms with a functional role, guiding people to the building's entrance. On the façade, an element specific to Romanian Brutalism is the integration of mural mosaics and reliefs, made by multidisciplinary teams of architects and visual artists.

Among the best-known examples is the Polyvalent Hall, designed by Nicolae Porumbescu. With its roof suspended from steel cables, it is probably the boldest example of structural Brutalism in the country, comparable with international achievements of the time. Other examples are the Intercontinental Hotel (cantilevers and deep loggias), the Romexpo Complex (prestressed concrete dome) and the Children's Palace.

Representative buildings:
  • Polyvalent Hall (Palace of Sports and Culture) | 1974 | arch. Nicolae Porumbescu | Parcul Tineretului, Intrarea Acvila 2
  • State Circus (today Globus) | 1960 | arch. Nicolae Porumbescu | Aleea Circului 15
  • Romexpo Complex | 1963–1964 | arch. Ascanio Damian & team | Bulevardul Mărășești 65-67

buildings.name: "Leu" Student Complex, Building A, Bulevardul Iuliu Maniu 1-3
Faculty of Architecture, new building. Strada Academiei 18-20

title: Contemporary
description: Bucharest's architecture after 1990 is hard to define by a common denominator. The lack of aesthetic consensus, real-estate market pressures and ever-shorter time horizons have produced a fragmented architectural output. The result is a set of distinct buildings that, more often than not, are not harmoniously integrated into the existing built fabric.

The architectural concept has become as important as society's attitude towards economic and cultural development. From the uncritical enthusiasm of the 1990s, through the corporate expansion after 2007, to authored architecture attentive to quality and sustainability, Bucharest has taken in a wide variety of buildings. At the same time, it can be said that responsibility towards the city and the landscape has become an increasingly visible attitude.

Defining architectural features:
  • Elements that make this architecture distinctive include the curtain wall, façades with parametric geometry and irregular volumes. The Barbu Văcărescu – Floreasca and Aurel Vlaicu – Pipera areas are already recognised as representative centres for this kind of architecture. Design produced with algorithmic design software can yield both buildings of remarkable quality and monotonous buildings with no clear intent, resulting in a heterogeneous and uneven fabric.
  • The need for sustainable design in architecture arose in response to climate change. Systems were adopted to improve buildings and fit them into this new context: ventilated façades, green roofs, photovoltaic panels and other green energy systems. Although these technologies are increasingly necessary for contemporary living, they can pose aesthetic challenges, especially in a historic fabric as diverse as Bucharest's.
  • Last but not least, the conversion of industrial heritage has led to the creation of creative hubs and coworking spaces, generating an interesting dialogue between old structures that have lost their original function and new programmes that need space for their activities.

Beyond these sub-currents, the common problem remains fitting new buildings into a city that is already densely built and whose population keeps growing. The problem is not just the quality of individual interventions, but the absence of an overall vision. As long as questions about the existing fabric and a minimum standard of quality for architectural design are ignored, the results at the scale of the neighbourhood or the city will remain fragmented and directionless.

title: Postmodern
description: Although in Bucharest it is part of the broader contemporary current, Postmodernism has distinctive features worth discussing separately. Internationally, Postmodernism emerged as an ironic response to the uniformity and monotony brought by Modernism. Postmodernism argues for rehabilitating history by reusing it as a legitimate source of inspiration. Modernism's supremacy of function and elimination of ornament no longer suited the cultural and historical context. Perhaps the best-known theorists of the movement were Robert Venturi in “Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture” (1966) and Charles Jencks in “The Language of Post-Modern Architecture” (1977). In their view, a building has a dual role: to embrace popular historical language while meeting the design standards of its time.

Bucharest took this direction in an unusual way, not so much as a reaction to a rigid, exhausted local modernism, but in connection with the collapse of communism. The style therefore offered a new form of freedom, an aesthetic freedom much needed after decades of socialist uniformity. Locally, however, unlike in the West, the style was not understood in all its dimensions, and was more often applied without critical filtering. In Bucharest, the style's reference period can be placed between 1990 and 2005.

Defining architectural features:
  • The ironic historical quotation is the defining feature of this style: a triangular pediment attached to the glass façade of an office building, columns marking a supermarket entrance, garish colours on buildings with important functions. This revival of elements from the past is not mainly meant to continue a tradition, but rather to make an aesthetic comment or to leave the creative gesture as free as possible.
  • Juxtaposed geometric forms are also used repeatedly: cylinders intersecting rectangular blocks, a pitched roof next to a flat terrace roof.

This period also saw the rise of mall architecture inspired directly by the American model, a stage-like space that combines “quotations” from every era inside. In Bucharest, the suburban residential architecture of the 2000s is what most often answers to this style, from villas with turrets and battlements to houses with garishly coloured façades.

Commercial examples include the World Trade Center Bucharest, the Marriott Hotel on Calea 13 Septembrie and the AFI Palace Cotroceni and Plaza România malls. Public buildings were also built in this period, such as the Boema Wing of the Central University Library and the High Court of Cassation and Justice. Setting aside personal taste, it can be said that the arrival of this style irreversibly marked today's local landscape, and it is associated with the post-communist transition.
